text: A COPY INTO transformation includes a GROUP BY clause to aggregate data during loading. What happens?

options.A: The data is aggregated and loaded successfully
options.B: The command FAILS — COPY transformations do NOT support GROUP BY (aggregate) syntax or JOINs
options.C: The GROUP BY is silently ignored and raw rows are loaded
options.D: The aggregation is applied but only for Parquet files

explanation: COPY INTO transformations support column reordering, casts, and a subset of scalar functions, but do NOT support GROUP BY, JOINs, FLATTEN, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, or DISTINCT. For aggregation during load, use a post-load transformation.

text: MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = 'CASE_INSENSITIVE' is specified in a COPY INTO statement that also includes a SELECT transformation. What happens?

options.A: Both work together — columns are matched by name and transformed
options.B: The command FAILS — MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME cannot be used together with a SELECT transformation in COPY INTO
options.C: MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME takes precedence and the SELECT is ignored
options.D: The SELECT takes precedence and MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME is ignored

explanation: You cannot combine MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME with a COPY transformation (SELECT statement). They are mutually exclusive. Use one approach or the other — not both.

text: An engineer loads CSV data with ERROR_ON_COLUMN_COUNT_MISMATCH = FALSE. A file has 5 fields but the table has 3 columns. What happens?

options.A: The load fails because the file has more fields than columns
options.B: The first 3 fields are loaded into the table columns in order; the remaining 2 fields are discarded
options.C: All 5 fields are loaded into new auto-created columns
options.D: The file is skipped

explanation: With ERROR_ON_COLUMN_COUNT_MISMATCH = FALSE: if the file has MORE fields than table columns, matching fields load in order and extra fields are discarded. If FEWER fields, remaining columns get NULL.

text: A COPY INTO statement includes TRUNCATECOLUMNS = TRUE. A string value in the file is 500 characters but the target VARCHAR column is 100. What happens?

options.A: An error is raised because the string exceeds column length
options.B: The string is automatically truncated to 100 characters and loaded without error
options.C: The entire file is skipped
options.D: The string is stored in an overflow column

explanation: TRUNCATECOLUMNS = TRUE automatically truncates strings exceeding the target column length. Default is FALSE (which raises an error). ENFORCE_LENGTH is the inverse parameter with opposite logic.

text: When unloading data with COPY INTO @stage, what is the default maximum file size per output file?

options.A: 64 MB
options.B: 16 MB
options.C: 128 MB
options.D: 1 GB

explanation: The default MAX_FILE_SIZE for COPY INTO <location> (unload) is 16 MB (16777216 bytes). The maximum allowed value is 5 GB. Snowflake splits output across multiple files based on this limit.

text: An engineer uses COPY INTO @stage with SINGLE = TRUE. What is the behavior?

options.A: Multiple files are created with sequential numbering
options.B: ALL data is unloaded into a SINGLE output file, named 'data' with no extension by default
options.C: Only one row is unloaded
options.D: The command fails because SINGLE requires a filename

explanation: SINGLE = TRUE generates one output file. By default it's named 'data' with no extension. To specify a name and extension, include it in the path (e.g., @stage/myfile.csv).

text: A sequence (seq1) is used in a COPY INTO transformation: SELECT seq1.nextval, $1, $2 FROM @stage. What does this achieve?

options.A: It errors because sequences cannot be used in COPY
options.B: It adds an auto-incrementing sequence value to each loaded row — useful for generating surrogate keys during load
options.C: It replaces the first column with a random number
options.D: It creates a new sequence for each file

explanation: Sequences CAN be used in COPY transformations via seq.nextval in the SELECT list. This generates a unique sequence value for each row loaded — useful for surrogate key assignment during bulk loading.

text: Which TWO metadata columns can be captured during a COPY INTO load? (Select TWO)

options.A: METADATA$FILENAME — the source file name
options.B: METADATA$WAREHOUSE — the warehouse processing the load
options.C: METADATA$START_SCAN_TIME — the time the file scan began (load timestamp)
options.D: METADATA$TABLE_NAME — the target table name

explanation: Available METADATA$ columns include: METADATA$FILENAME, METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER, METADATA$FILE_CONTENT_KEY, METADATA$FILE_LAST_MODIFIED, and METADATA$START_SCAN_TIME. There is no METADATA$WAREHOUSE or METADATA$TABLE_NAME.

text: COPY INTO unloads data to Parquet format. The source table has a VARIANT column. How is it represented in the Parquet output?

options.A: The VARIANT column is dropped from the output
options.B: The VARIANT column is converted into a simple JSON string in the Parquet file
options.C: The VARIANT is stored as a nested Parquet struct automatically
options.D: An error is raised because VARIANT cannot be unloaded to Parquet

explanation: When unloading to CSV, JSON, or Parquet, VARIANT columns are converted into simple JSON strings. Nested data in VARIANT cannot be automatically converted to nested Parquet structures.

text: SIZE_LIMIT = 25000000 is set on a COPY INTO statement loading from a stage with many 10 MB files. How many files are loaded?

options.A: Exactly 2 files (20 MB < 25 MB)
options.B: 3 files — loading continues until the cumulative size EXCEEDS the threshold, then stops. At least one file always loads.
options.C: All files regardless of size limit
options.D: Only the first file

explanation: SIZE_LIMIT specifies the maximum cumulative data size. Loading continues until the threshold is exceeded, then discontinues. With 10 MB files and 25 MB limit: file 1 (10), file 2 (20), file 3 (30 > 25) — 3 files load before stopping.

text: A task DAG has a root task and 3 child tasks (A, B, C). Tasks A and B are children of root. Task C has AFTER task_a, task_b. When does task C execute?

options.A: When either A or B completes
options.B: Only when BOTH A and B complete successfully — a task with multiple predecessors waits for ALL resumed predecessors to succeed
options.C: Immediately after the root task
options.D: After whichever finishes last, regardless of success

explanation: When a task has multiple predecessors, it waits for ALL resumed predecessors to successfully complete. If either A or B fails, task C does not execute (unless the failed task is suspended).

text: What is a finalizer task in a task DAG?

options.A: A task that runs before the root task
options.B: An optional task that runs AFTER all other tasks complete or fail — used for cleanup, notifications, or error correction
options.C: A task that validates the DAG structure
options.D: A task that automatically suspends the DAG

explanation: A finalizer task (CREATE TASK ... FINALIZE = root_task) runs after ALL other tasks in the graph complete or fail. It's used for cleanup operations, sending notifications, or correcting errors. Each root task can have only one finalizer.

text: A task graph fails. The parameter TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 2 is set on the root task. What happens?

options.A: Only the failed child task retries twice
options.B: The ENTIRE task graph is immediately retried up to 2 times. If it still fails after retries, the graph is considered failed.
options.C: The root task retries but children do not
options.D: Nothing — auto-retry only works for standalone tasks

explanation: TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS on the root task causes the entire task graph to be retried when a child task fails. The full graph reruns from the beginning, up to the specified number of attempts.

text: SUSPEND_TASK_AFTER_NUM_FAILURES = 3 is set on a root task. After how many consecutive failures is the task graph automatically suspended?

options.A: After the first failure
options.B: After 3 consecutive task graph failures — the task graph is automatically suspended to prevent ongoing credit waste
options.C: After 10 failures (default, ignoring the parameter)
options.D: Never — tasks must be manually suspended

explanation: SUSPEND_TASK_AFTER_NUM_FAILURES suspends the task graph after the specified number of consecutive failures or timeouts. Default is 10. Setting it to 3 means auto-suspension after 3 consecutive failures.

text: SYSTEM$TASK_DEPENDENTS_ENABLE('root_task') is called. What does this function do?

options.A: It drops all child tasks
options.B: It RESUMES the root task AND all child tasks (including the finalizer) in the task graph simultaneously
options.C: It only resumes the root task
options.D: It enables monitoring on the task graph

explanation: SYSTEM$TASK_DEPENDENTS_ENABLE resumes the root task AND all its dependent/child tasks at once. This is a convenience function that avoids resuming each task individually.

text: A child task in a DAG calls SYSTEM$GET_PREDECESSOR_RETURN_VALUE('PARENT_TASK'). What does this retrieve?

options.A: The SQL text of the parent task
options.B: The RETURN VALUE set by the parent task using SYSTEM$SET_RETURN_VALUE — enabling inter-task communication
options.C: The execution duration of the parent task
options.D: The error message from the parent task

explanation: Tasks can pass data to their children using SYSTEM$SET_RETURN_VALUE (in the parent) and SYSTEM$GET_PREDECESSOR_RETURN_VALUE (in the child). This enables logic-based inter-task communication within a DAG.

text: A task is configured with EXECUTE AS USER task_user. How does this differ from the default behavior?

options.A: No difference — tasks always run as a user
options.B: Default: tasks run as a system service with the owner role's privileges. EXECUTE AS USER: tasks run on behalf of a specific user, inheriting their privileges and appearing in audit logs under their identity.
options.C: EXECUTE AS USER requires ACCOUNTADMIN
options.D: EXECUTE AS USER makes the task serverless

explanation: By default, tasks run as a system service (no specific user). EXECUTE AS USER makes the task run on behalf of a named user, which is useful for data masking policies that depend on the querying user, and for audit trail attribution.

text: What is the maximum number of tasks allowed in a single task graph (DAG)?

options.D: Unlimited

explanation: A task graph is limited to a maximum of 1000 tasks. Additionally, a single task can have at most 100 parent tasks and 100 child tasks.

text: A stream is created on a view (not a table). Is this supported?

options.A: No — streams can only be created on tables
options.B: Yes — streams can be created on views, but only if CHANGE_TRACKING = TRUE is enabled on the underlying tables
options.C: Yes — but only on secure views
options.D: Yes — but only on materialized views

explanation: Streams can be created on views, but the underlying tables referenced by the view must have CHANGE_TRACKING = TRUE enabled. This allows the stream to track changes through the view.

text: An engineer queries a table using the CHANGES clause: SELECT * FROM my_table CHANGES(INFORMATION => DEFAULT) AT(OFFSET => -300). What does this return?

options.A: The current table data
options.B: The change records (inserts/updates/deletes) that occurred in the last 300 seconds — WITHOUT requiring a stream object
options.C: Historical data from 300 seconds ago
options.D: An error because CHANGES requires a stream

explanation: The CHANGES clause on a table (with CHANGE_TRACKING = TRUE) returns change records without requiring a separate stream object. It uses AT/BEFORE to define the time window. Unlike streams, it does NOT advance any offset.

text: A dynamic table pipeline has 3 levels: DT_A → DT_B → DT_C. DT_A has TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM, DT_B has TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM, DT_C has TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'. How is DT_A refreshed?

options.A: DT_A never refreshes because it has no independent lag
options.B: DT_A refreshes to satisfy the 5-minute lag of its downstream consumer DT_C — Snowflake propagates the lag requirement UP the chain
options.C: DT_A refreshes every 1 minute (minimum)
options.D: DT_A only refreshes when manually triggered

explanation: TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM means the table has no independent schedule. Snowflake propagates the lag requirement from the furthest downstream consumer (DT_C at 5 min) up through the pipeline, scheduling refreshes as needed to meet that target.

text: Can a dynamic table be used as the source for a stream?

options.A: No — streams cannot track changes on dynamic tables
options.B: Yes — streams can be created on dynamic tables to capture their refresh changes
options.C: Only append-only streams work on dynamic tables
options.D: Only if the dynamic table has a clustering key

explanation: Streams CAN be created on dynamic tables. Each time the dynamic table refreshes, the stream captures the net changes. This allows combining dynamic tables with task-based processing downstream.

text: What privilege must the task OWNER role have at the ACCOUNT level for the task to actually execute?

options.A: CREATE TASK
options.B: EXECUTE TASK — without this account-level privilege, the task will not run even if properly created and resumed
options.C: MONITOR
options.D: OPERATE

explanation: The task owner role needs EXECUTE TASK at the account level for tasks to run. Additionally, serverless tasks need EXECUTE MANAGED TASK. Without EXECUTE TASK, the task is created and resumed but will not execute.

text: A triggered task is created: CREATE TASK my_task WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('my_stream') AS .... No SCHEDULE is defined. How is this task executed?

options.A: It never runs because there is no schedule
options.B: It runs as a triggered task — Snowflake automatically checks the stream condition and fires the task when data is available, without a fixed schedule
options.C: It runs every 1 minute by default
options.D: It only runs when manually executed

explanation: Triggered tasks (with WHEN but no SCHEDULE) are event-driven. Snowflake monitors the condition and fires the task when it evaluates to TRUE. This eliminates polling and reduces latency for stream-based processing.

text: EXECUTE TASK my_root_task is called while the root task is suspended. What happens?

options.A: An error — tasks cannot be executed while suspended
options.B: A single instance of the task graph runs immediately — EXECUTE TASK works on suspended tasks for testing purposes
options.C: The task is automatically resumed permanently
options.D: Nothing — the command is ignored

explanation: EXECUTE TASK runs a single instance of the task graph regardless of the task's suspended/resumed state. This is designed for testing new or modified task graphs before enabling them in production.

text: Which TWO parameters control the compute size of a serverless task? (Select TWO)

options.A: WAREHOUSE_SIZE
options.B: SERVERLESS_TASK_MIN_STATEMENT_SIZE — minimum warehouse size floor
options.C: SERVERLESS_TASK_MAX_STATEMENT_SIZE — maximum warehouse size ceiling
options.D: USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE — initial size (legacy)

explanation: Serverless tasks use SERVERLESS_TASK_MIN_STATEMENT_SIZE (floor, default XSMALL) and SERVERLESS_TASK_MAX_STATEMENT_SIZE (ceiling, default XXLARGE). Snowflake auto-scales between these. USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE is the legacy parameter.

text: A storage integration specifies STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://bucket-a/prod/', 's3://bucket-b/'). A stage references s3://bucket-a/dev/. Can data be loaded from this stage?

options.A: Yes — the integration allows all paths under bucket-a
options.B: No — STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS restricts access to specific paths. 's3://bucket-a/dev/' is NOT within 's3://bucket-a/prod/'
options.C: Yes — path prefixes are ignored for allowed locations
options.D: No — only one bucket can be specified per integration

explanation: STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS enforces path-level restrictions. 's3://bucket-a/prod/' only allows access to paths starting with /prod/. The path /dev/ is not covered, so access is denied.

text: An Azure-based Snowflake account uses AUTO_INGEST = TRUE for Snowpipe. Which Azure service delivers file arrival notifications?

options.A: Azure Functions
options.B: Azure Event Grid (via blob storage events)
options.C: Azure Service Bus
options.D: Azure Logic Apps

explanation: For Azure auto-ingest, Snowpipe uses Azure Event Grid. Blob storage generates events when new files arrive, and Event Grid routes them to Snowpipe via a storage queue. This is analogous to SQS for AWS and Pub/Sub for GCP.

text: An engineer checks pipe status using the insertReport REST API endpoint. What information does it provide?

options.A: The SQL definition of the pipe
options.B: The status of files submitted to Snowpipe — whether they are queued, loading, loaded, or failed
options.C: The warehouse credit consumption
options.D: The stage file listing

explanation: The insertReport endpoint provides status information about files submitted to Snowpipe: whether files are queued, currently loading, successfully loaded, or failed. It's used for monitoring and debugging ingestion pipelines.

text: A pipe has ERROR_INTEGRATION set. What does this enable?

options.A: Automatic error correction during loading
options.B: Notification delivery (email or webhook) when Snowpipe encounters ingestion errors — alerts the team to failures
options.C: Routing of error rows to a quarantine table
options.D: Automatic retry of failed files

explanation: ERROR_INTEGRATION specifies a notification integration that sends alerts when Snowpipe encounters errors. This enables proactive monitoring — teams are notified of failures via email or webhook without polling.

text: VALIDATE(my_table, job_id => last_query_id()) is called after a COPY INTO. What does it return?

options.A: The row count of loaded data
options.B: All errors encountered during the specified COPY operation — row-level error details for debugging
options.C: A boolean (TRUE/FALSE) indicating success
options.D: The schema of the loaded file

explanation: The VALIDATE function returns detailed error information (row number, column, error message) from a specific COPY job. It ONLY works for standard COPY loads — not for COPY with transformations (SELECT).

text: LOAD_UNCERTAIN_FILES = TRUE is specified. What does this option do?

options.A: Forces loading of all files regardless of previous load status
options.B: Loads files whose load status is UNKNOWN (metadata expired after 64 days) — files that COPY would normally skip due to uncertainty
options.C: Loads encrypted files without decryption keys
options.D: Loads files with schema mismatches

explanation: After 64 days, file load metadata expires and status becomes 'unknown'. COPY normally skips these files. LOAD_UNCERTAIN_FILES = TRUE forces loading of files with unknown status. FORCE = TRUE is broader — it loads ALL files regardless.

text: INCLUDE_QUERY_ID = TRUE is set on a COPY INTO @stage (unload). What does this add to output filenames?

options.A: A timestamp
options.B: A UUID (the query ID of the COPY statement) — ensuring unique filenames and preventing overwrites from concurrent operations
options.C: The table name
options.D: A sequential counter

explanation: INCLUDE_QUERY_ID = TRUE adds a UUID (the COPY statement's query ID) to output filenames. This prevents concurrent unload operations from overwriting each other's files and aids cleanup if operations fail.

text: A root task has CONFIG = '{"env": "prod", "batch_size": 1000}'. How can a child task read this configuration?

options.A: SELECT CONFIG FROM TASK_METADATA
options.B: SELECT SYSTEM$GET_TASK_GRAPH_CONFIG('env') — retrieves the value for a specific key from the graph-level config
options.C: SELECT TASK_CONFIG()
options.D: The config is automatically available as session variables

explanation: SYSTEM$GET_TASK_GRAPH_CONFIG(key) retrieves configuration values from the root task's CONFIG JSON. This enables graph-level configuration that all child tasks can read — useful for environment settings, paths, etc.

text: The OVERLAP_POLICY parameter on a root task is set to ALLOW_CHILD_OVERLAP. What does this mean?

options.A: Child tasks can run in parallel with each other (they already can)
options.B: When the next scheduled root task fires while child tasks are still running, a NEW instance of the root task starts — but root tasks never overlap with themselves
options.C: Multiple root task instances can run simultaneously
options.D: Tasks from different DAGs can share compute

explanation: ALLOW_CHILD_OVERLAP: if children are still running when the next scheduled time arrives, a new graph instance starts from the root. Root tasks don't overlap with this policy. NO_OVERLAP (default): waits for all tasks to finish. ALLOW_ALL_OVERLAP: true parallelism.

text: What is the maximum compute size for a serverless task?

options.A: XL (16 credits/hour equivalent)
options.B: XXLARGE — equivalent to a 2XL warehouse. Workloads requiring more must use user-managed warehouses.
options.C: 4XL (128 credits/hour equivalent)
options.D: Unlimited — Snowflake scales automatically

explanation: Serverless tasks have a maximum compute equivalent of XXLARGE (2XL). If a workload needs more compute than this, you must use a user-managed task with a larger warehouse (3XL or 4XL).

text: A task graph's root task is suspended. Are running child tasks immediately cancelled?

options.A: Yes — all tasks stop immediately when root is suspended
options.B: No — if tasks are currently running, they complete their current execution. Only FUTURE scheduled runs are cancelled.
options.C: Child tasks are paused mid-execution and resume when root resumes
options.D: Only the finalizer is cancelled

explanation: Suspending the root task cancels all future scheduled runs but does NOT interrupt currently executing tasks. Running tasks and their descendants complete their current execution using the current version.

text: INSERT-ONLY streams can be created on which special table types?

options.A: Only permanent tables
options.B: External tables and Iceberg tables — where only INSERT operations are possible (no UPDATE/DELETE)
options.C: Dynamic tables only
options.D: Temporary tables only

explanation: Insert-only streams are specifically for external tables and Iceberg tables, where only INSERT operations occur (data is append-only from external sources). Standard and append-only streams are for regular tables.

text: A Git integration is created in Snowflake. What does it provide?

options.A: Automatic deployment of dbt models from Git
options.B: The ability to sync code files from a Git repository into a Snowflake stage — version-controlling SQL, Python, and other files
options.C: Real-time streaming of Git commit data
options.D: GitHub issue tracking within Snowflake

explanation: Git integrations sync files from a Git repository into a Snowflake stage. This enables version-controlled SQL scripts, Python code, and configuration files to be accessible within Snowflake for use in tasks, procedures, and notebooks.

text: A COPY INTO command references a stage with a PATTERN clause: PATTERN = '.*sales.*[.]csv'. What files are loaded?

options.A: Only files named exactly 'sales.csv'
options.B: All files whose names match the regex — any file containing 'sales' with a .csv extension (the brackets escape the dot)
options.C: Files in the 'sales' directory only
options.D: All CSV files regardless of name

explanation: PATTERN uses regex matching. '.*sales.*[.]csv' matches any file containing 'sales' with .csv extension. '.*' = any characters, [.] escapes the literal dot. This filters which staged files are included in the load.
